beats.say: Dollar Tree sells everything for a single price. And that price keeps moving.
A handful of shelves hold higher-priced items you can't find elsewhere.
The bulk of the store stays stocked with the classic low-cost goods.
A tiny section offers a few premium picks at a steeper tag.
Since 2019 the store slipped $3 and $5 items onto the floor. Looks like a mistake.
But it does a job - it creates a price anchor.
The anchor makes the $1.25 baseline feel cheap, even though it's a 25% hike after 35 years.
Shoppers compare every aisle to the $3-$5 items, so the $1.25 feels like a bargain.
The $1 items become the default choice, hiding the price increase.
You see it everywhere. A coffee shop lists a $2 regular brew, a $3 specialty, and a $5 premium blend.
A gym shows a $10 day pass, a $15 weekly pass, and a $30 monthly membership.
Because the $15 weekly looks modest next to $30 monthly, the $10 day pass feels like the smart pick.
When a menu adds a pricier decoy, the middle price will look like a deal. Follow for more.
